sections.heading: 01 — Core Principles
sections.intro:
Five patterns recur across this collection often enough to treat as load-bearing, even though no
single source states them as a numbered list. Read these first — they're the lens the rest of this
package applies to any specific movement, drill, or practice.

---

subsections.body:
The recurring claim across this collection's coaching and founder-level sources is that running,
jumping, climbing, throwing, and carrying are the ancestral, general-purpose movement repertoire
humans evolved with — and that specific sports (soccer, tennis, weightlifting) are narrower,
specialized expressions of that same underlying capability, not the other way around. One source
puts it directly: sport and fitness "enable natural movement" only in the sense that natural
movement is what "make[s] any sports... any physical activity... possible" in the first place, since
"our ancestors evolved with these abilities" long before any sport formalized a narrow slice of
them.
subsections.heading: 1. Natural movement is framed as the origin sport and exercise are derived from, not the reverse

subsections.body:
Several sources draw a sharp line between "exercise" (repetition performed for its own sake,
described in this collection as potentially "mindless") and "practicing movement" (engaging with a
real physical problem — getting up off the floor, carrying a load, crossing an obstacle). This
distinction is used as a diagnostic tool as much as a philosophy: how a person solves the "get up
off the floor" problem, and which solution they avoid, is treated as revealing something concrete
about their mobility or strength that a repetition-based exercise wouldn't surface.
subsections.heading: 2. Movement is framed as a behavior that solves a real problem, not a repetition to perform

subsections.body:
More than one source is explicit that natural movement is not the same as unstructured outdoor
play — it's taught as a systematic method with progressions, the same way a martial art is taught
through trained technique rather than improvised fighting. This collection's sources are
consistent that movements which look effortless on video (a barefoot rock-face slide, a smooth
get-up) are effortless *because* of trained technique, not because they require no skill — a point
several sources say surprises people who try to replicate the movements without preparation.
subsections.heading: 3. Technique and structured progression matter even for "natural" movement

subsections.body:
A specific, repeated caution across barefoot training, spinal mobility, and general movement
coaching in this collection is that skipping a gradual buildup is the direct cause of overuse
injury (hairline fractures, plantar fasciitis, tendinitis are named examples). The stated mechanism
is that years of cushioned, unchallenged movement dull tissue tolerance, so tolerance has to be
rebuilt in small doses rather than assumed to already be present. A closely related, separately
stated principle for mobility work specifically: "frequency or consistency" beats intensity —
light, frequent practice is described as more effective than infrequent, aggressive stretching.
subsections.heading: 4. Capacity has to be built gradually — the body has been "numbed," and rushing causes injury

subsections.body:
Multiple sources in this collection push back against relying on external leverage (pulling on a
limb, using momentum) as the main driver of a mobility gain, instead directing attention to
visualizing the body's internal shape and using the person's own muscular tension to reach an end
range. The stated reasoning is that awareness — recognizing where a limitation actually lives, not
just pushing harder at the point that's already flexible — is what produces lasting change, with
the stretch or the load treated as the occasion for that awareness rather than the mechanism on its
own.
subsections.heading: 5. Awareness and self-generated effort are treated as doing more than the stretch or load itself

sections.heading: 02 — Daily Practices
sections.intro:
A by-practice lookup pulling together the concrete, repeatable drills this collection covers. This
is a summary for quick orientation — the individual notes carry the full detail, direct quotation,
and timestamps this file leaves out. Nothing here is medical or injury-rehab advice; where a
practice risks strain, the caution given by the source is repeated here too.

---

subsections.body:
Practiced as a training pattern: from lying down, shift body weight onto a bent leg to roll to the
side, transfer weight to the elbow, then the hand, move into a half-kneeling position, and stand —
reversing the sequence to return to the floor. Tools (a kettlebell held overhead, a heavy sandbag)
are used as *teaching constraints*, not as the point of the exercise — the actual goal is always
"can you get up off the floor," not how much weight you can get up with.

The same movement doubles as a **self-check**: which of the few ways of standing up you default to
— and which you avoid — is a plain-language signal of where a limitation might be. Defaulting to a
split-squat stance and never accessing a full squat position when getting up, for instance, points
toward checking ankle or hip mobility rather than assuming it's just "how you get up."
subsections.heading: The get-up (as a daily movement, and as a self-check)

subsections.body:
Start with **foot-specific drills**, not by simply removing shoes and running: toe yoga (moving
toes independently), toe drops (lifting all toes, lowering one at a time from the outside in), "toe
rainbow" (pushing the big and little toes down while lifting the middle three), "short foot"
(lifting the arch without curling the toes), and balance work on elevated or unstable surfaces.

Once foot strength is being built, add barefoot conditioning in **short intervals**, not a
continuous run — alternate a short bout of barefoot running/shuffling with a different modality
(rowing, cycling, a ski erg) rather than running the full session barefoot. Progress gradually:
skipping this buildup is named as the direct cause of stress fractures, plantar fasciitis, and
tendinitis in runners who switch too fast. Match the surface to the practice — a natural surface
(grass) is treated as appropriate; hot or debris-covered pavement is not.
subsections.heading: Barefoot training (building it up safely)

subsections.body:
1. **Rotation** — sit elevated (hips at or above knee height) for a neutral spine, then reach
   backward in sequence: head, then torso, then arm. Hold the end-range rotation for about 10
   seconds using your own muscular tension, not by pulling with the opposite hand.
2. **Flexion (rocking)** — flex the spine into a "C" shape working upper back, then mid/lower back,
   then the hips, and rock gently with minimal arm/leg momentum. If the rock feels jarring rather
   than smooth, it's a sign one spinal segment (often the lower back) isn't sharing the flexion
   evenly with the rest.
3. **Extension (prone lying)** — from forearms, press up onto the wrists while looking up to extend
   the upper back. If the stretch is felt mainly in the lower back or the neck instead, that's
   named as a sign the mid/upper back isn't doing its share — back off and redirect the extension
   there rather than pushing further.

Governing principle for all three: **frequency over intensity** — light, daily (even multiple
times daily) practice is described as producing better results than infrequent, hard stretching
sessions.
subsections.heading: Spinal mobility (three movements, in order: rotation, flexion, extension)

subsections.body:
If a get-up or squat check points to a limited ankle or hip: kneeling ankle self-mobilization using
body weight; a toe-inclusive rocking drill; a seated position (sitting on one shin, other foot
forward) with the knee gliding over the toes in a "rainbow" arc; a tall half-kneel with reaching in
multiple directions to shift body weight; and a pull-assisted deep squat with side-to-side weight
shifting at the bottom. All of these are done slowly, breathing through the nose, without forcing —
the stated reason is to avoid triggering a protective, guarding response in the nervous system.
subsections.heading: Ankle and hip mobility drills (for a limited get-up or squat pattern)

**Differential learning** — deliberately varying a movement slightly on each repetition (e.g.
moving a hand's position) to expose a learner to more variation rather than one fixed pattern.

**Emulation** — the term used for the peer-engagement effect of training natural movement in a
large group rather than alone.

subsections.body:
**Natural method** — the roughly hundred-year-old French physical education tradition based on
Georges Hébert's work, distinct from and older than MovNat.

subsections.body:

- **Main subjects:** three natural-movement drills for spinal mobility, one each for rotation, flexion, and extension, taught with an emphasis on body awareness over stretch amplitude
- **Movements & practices:** rotation: seated on an elevated bolster (hips above knee height) for a neutral spine, then reaching backward in sequence (head, then torso, then arm), holding an end-range rotation for 10 seconds using the body's own muscular tension rather than pulling with the opposite hand, flexion (rocking): forward-flexing the spine into a "C" shape (upper back, then mid/lower back, then hips) and rocking gently using minimal arm/leg momentum, then holding a full flexed position for 10 seconds, extension (prone lying): from forearms, pressing up onto the wrists while looking upward to extend the upper back, steering the extension away from the lower back or neck if felt there, then holding an extended position for 10 seconds using upper-back strength rather than pressing hard off the ground
- **Evolutionary principles:** "the key to success of mobility is more about frequency or consistency than it is about intensity" — light, frequent daily practice recommended over occasional intense stretching, awareness and visualization (imagining the spine as a pole or ladder) are presented as more responsible for gained mobility than the stretch itself, since they direct effort toward stiff segments rather than over-stretching already-mobile ones
- **Important concepts:** segmental spinal movement — the idea that a stretch should be distributed evenly across every vertebral segment (base of skull to lower back) rather than concentrated in the most flexible area

- **Movements & practices:** floor and ground positions (including a figure-four position) used by MovNat's performance director Brian Betancourt himself to regain range of motion and confidence after a severe knee ligament injury, approached gradually with physical therapist guidance

- **Important concepts:** Ryan Peters' account of discovering MovNat through a chapter on natural movement in "The Paleo Manifesto" by John Durant, leading him from conventional strength training into natural movement as a physical therapist and running coach, Brian Betancourt's own knee injury (described as LCL, PCL, and MCL damage graded "two plus," with a subluxation/dislocation and only the ACL intact) used as a first-person case study for natural-movement-based rehabilitation

- **Duration:** 23:18

- **Main subjects:** a full guided restoration practice moving through lying, floor-sitting, kneeling, squatting, and standing positions, framed as reconnecting practitioners to "elementary positions and transitions that we've lost in our modern lives"
- **Movements & practices:** a supine breathing/alignment position (the source's own term, heard in the transcript as "move notot," likely a caption mishearing of a named position) — midback and back of the neck on the ground, chin tucked, shoulders rolled away from the midline, 10 breaths, then reaching overhead for 5 more, side-rolling from supine to prone and back, leading with the arms and then with the legs, keeping the hips glued to the ground while reaching across the body, a prone-to-push-up progression: forearm-supported extension, rocking hips to heels and back, then walking the hands back toward the feet into a hip-elevated forward-fold position, ground-sitting transitions — cross-legged sit, side-bent sit, bent sit, and long sit — each focused on stacking the hips under the ribs rather than tucking them, the "tripod transition": posting one arm, externally rotating the elbow to point with the fingers, and rotating on the ball of one foot to move between ground positions, a kneeling progression from deep kneeling to tall kneeling to tall half-kneeling to a deep squat, then standing, a wall alignment exercise — hips, mid-back, and back of the head all touching a wall simultaneously — used to teach what the source calls an "ideal standing position", hip hinges against the wall and leg swings, closing with a 10-minute walk outdoors
- **Evolutionary principles:** breath-led relaxation and visualization (growing "longer, taller, wider") are used throughout to guide positioning, rather than forcing a stretch to a target range of motion, the wall-alignment exercise is explicitly framed as correcting a habitual forward-flexed posture: "this is what an ideal standing position would be if we weren't always forward flexed all the time", the practice explicitly closes by carrying its effects into ordinary movement (a walk) rather than ending the session self-contained
- **Important concepts:** the iliac crest and pubic bone alignment used as a specific anatomical landmark for judging correct kneeling posture

- **Movements & practices:** the "spinal engine" as the origin point of locomotion, developed (in Weck's evolutionary account) from lateral fish undulation through amphibian and mammalian strategies toward upright bipedal movement — presented as why the spine should be trained through multi-axis movement rather than braced into one "neutral" position, "balance begins in the upper body": Weck's claim that head/upper-body positioning determines how well the feet can do their job, attributed to faster nerve-signal transmission from the cervical spine than from the lumbar spine and to the head's greater degrees of freedom, ground-contact time in sprinting versus multidirectional sport: sprinters minimize ground contact to maximize flight time and stride length, while an example team-sport athlete (Tyreek Hill) is described as spending far more time on the ground, which Weck frames as trading top-end speed for the ability to change direction while still in contact with the ground, a reorganization of Georges Hébert's ten natural-method categories (walk, run, jump, climb, quadrupedal movement, balance, swim, lift, throw, defend) into broader groups — locomotion, manipulation of objects, interaction/play, and combat — with lifting and carrying stones as Weck's substitute for a barbell deadlift
- **Evolutionary principles:** "the caveman did not run away from the saber-tooth tiger" — Weck's claim that turning to flee a pursuing predator triggers its chase instinct, and that the evolutionarily sound response to a dangerous predator was group confrontation with weapons, not sprinting away, evolution is explicitly named by Weck as a useful but not literally true framework — "it's a theory that is wrong that is useful for the mental gymnastics of understanding yourself" — offered as his own epistemic hedge on the evolutionary narrative he builds the rest of the conversation on, a critique of mainstream strength and conditioning for prioritizing "mirror muscle" strength (chest, shoulders, glutes) over what Weck calls spine/hands/feet/neck strength, and for treating "stiffness" as the primary goal rather than coordinated, tone-based balance
- **Important concepts:** "tone" as the deepest, most chronic layer of muscular control (distinguished from phasic muscle contraction), which Weck connects — via his own therapy experience, not a cited study — to stored emotional trauma, CCT ("coiling core training") versus RMT ("rotational movement training") as Weck's own coined distinction between staying on one side while shifting weight (CCT) and crossing to the opposite side (RMT), "stick, rope, and rock" as Weck's distilled account of humanity's original tools/toys, offered as the basis for manipulative movement training in place of gym equipment

sections.body:
**This is a full guided restoration practice — moving through lying, ground-sitting, kneeling,
squatting, and standing positions — explicitly framed as reconnecting a practitioner to
"elementary positions and transitions that we've lost in our modern lives," prioritizing breath
and awareness-led positioning over forcing range of motion.** `[00:02]` "This natural movement
primary series is a dedicated sequence of movements that reconnects us to the elementary positions
and transitions that we've lost in our modern lives, from lying to floor sitting to standing and
even breathing... this practice is for rebuilding and maintaining fundamental levels of mobility
and body control for the beginner and advanced natural movement practitioner alike."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:02]`–`[02:03]` The practice opens lying on the back, working toward a named alignment position
(heard in the transcript as "the move notot position" — likely a caption mishearing of a specific
named term this source uses, reproduced here as heard since the correct term can't be confirmed):
midback and the back of the neck touching the ground, chin tucked, shoulders rolled so the thumbs
point toward the ceiling, held for 10 breaths and then 5 more with the arms swept overhead.
Breathing is directed specifically into "the three-dimensional space right where your ribs meet
your upper belly," with an instruction to keep breath "out of the collar bones and neck."
sections.heading: Opening position and breath

sections.body:
`[08:16]`–`[15:26]` A sequence of ground-sitting positions (cross-legged, side-bent, bent, long
sit) is built around one consistent target: "sit equally into both hip bones," with hips stacked
under the ribs rather than tucked. This transitions through a "tripod transition" (posting one arm,
rotating the elbow to point with the fingers, pivoting on the ball of the foot) into a kneeling
progression — deep kneeling, tall kneeling (checking that "the iliac crest is roughly in line with
your pubic bone"), tall half-kneeling with a stated counter-rotation cue (front knee rolling away
from the midline while the back knee spreads the opposite way), and finally a deep squat.
sections.heading: Ground-sitting and the kneeling-to-squat progression

sections.body:
`[18:32]`–`[19:32]` Standing against a wall, hips first, then the space below the shoulder blades,
then the back of the head, chin tucked — held for 10 breaths, then extended overhead reach while
maintaining midback and head contact. The source is explicit about what this position represents:
**"this is what an ideal standing position would be if we weren't always forward flexed all the
time."**

**The guest frames human physical capability around the idea of a shared, physically robust
ancestor — "our natural state is healthy... our natural state is robust if we don't get in our own
way" — and argues that general movement competency (not specialized strength) is the foundation
that should come first, illustrated by a strong lifter failing a basic floor get-up that he
performed smoothly.** `[12:14]` "I believe that we all stem from a common ancestor more or less
that was wildly robust, physically capable, and could thermoregulate on levels that we can't even
imagine today... our natural state is healthy. Our natural state is robust if we don't get in our
own way. And that goes for movement, in our environment, diet, lifestyle, toxin, relationships, all
that stuff."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[21:23]`–`[23:24]` At a strength-training certification, the guest describes watching a man who
"back squats 600 lb" and "looks like a ninja turtle" struggle with the get-up's elbow roll-up to
hand post, while he himself performed it smoothly enough that the instructor stopped the room to
point it out. His stated takeaway: **"if you improve the human generally with natural movement...
general human capacity, then you tend to alleviate peripheral symptoms and issues, but then once
you start to get into specializing, you're going to inevitably start to sacrifice general
capacities... I think that people specialize at the detriment of generality when general skills and
capacities can actually push specialization higher than they believe."** He immediately hedges this
as a debatable threshold, not a fixed rule: "that threshold is something to be debated."
sections.heading: The generalist-vs-specialist argument, and the get-up anecdote

sections.body:
`[42:46]`–`[44:50]` The guest's stated framework for coaching: "I think about physical practice as
a relationship with self... everyone has a physical practice. Whether or not they recognize that
they do." He argues disciplines like parkour, jiu-jitsu, and martial arts are valuable specifically
because they don't allow self-deception: **"these sorts of disciplines don't have much room for...
lies, because if you can't do something and you physically attempt it, you get shut down real quick
by gravity or the biggest guy in the room."** He contrasts this with martial artists who "just do
katas and believe they're the baddest guy in the room, but they've never actually fought."
`[58:01]` He states the physical and mental cannot be rightfully separated, framing broader
interest in movement training as a needed correction to that separation.
sections.heading: Physical practice as "a relationship with self"

sections.body:

fast-failure training device: "the only way you fail is if you don't throw the balls... with
juggling, you throw the balls and you drop them immediately. You're failing... paying attention to
what your goal is with each throw, and you're just failing, failing, failing. Then you get it."
He's explicit that failing alone isn't the lesson — it must be paired with diagnosis: "fail fast,
learn from it, take from it, change what you do. Don't fail the same way over and over again."

**Getting up off the floor without using the hands is presented as a movement-competency
assessment in its own right: because there are only a handful of ways to solve the "get up"
problem, which pattern a person defaults to — and which they avoid — reveals a specific mobility or
strength limitation without needing a full clinical test battery.** `[15:20]` "Movement is a

`[04:10]`–`[05:10]` The core logic: "when someone is getting off of the ground, they're going to
bias whatever they feel safe doing." If someone always rises via a split squat and avoids a full
squat pattern, the stated question becomes "why are you avoiding the squat" — pointing toward
ankle, hip, or knee mobility as the likely culprit, to be confirmed with a targeted screen rather
than assumed.

`[06:11]`–`[09:14]` Demonstrated on a case example ("Michaela," who consistently avoided the deep
squat): a 5-inch wall/PVC-pipe test screens ankle dorsiflexion in half-kneeling (driving the knee
toward the target without the heel lifting); passive joint-capsule and muscle-tightness checks
follow if the wall test is limited. For the hip, passive external rotation is tested at 90° hip
flexion, then compared against active external rotation from a seated position — **"if her active
range equals her passive range, then it's good. If her passive range is greater than her active
range, then it's a motor coordination problem"** requiring strengthening rather than stretching.
sections.heading: Confirming the hypothesis: ankle and hip screens

ankle self-mobilization using body weight, a toe-inclusive rocking drill, a seated position sitting

tall half-kneel with multidirectional reaching to shift body weight, and a pull-assisted deep squat
with side-to-side weight shifting at the bottom position — each performed slowly, with nasal
breathing and no forced strain, "so that nervous system" doesn't "kick in and start guarding."

**Erwan Le Corre describes making "The Workout The World Forgot" specifically to showcase natural,
evolutionary, ancestral movement — practiced outdoors and barefoot rather than in a gym — as
something he frames as every person's "birthright," suppressed by modern life rather than actually
lost.** `[06:11]` "It's about exercising, but exercising in nature and also based on completely
natural, evolutionary, ancestral movements... how about we move the way we're meant to move, we

sections.body:
`[01:01]`–`[03:05]` Le Corre made an early, "very amateur" version of the video in Corsica in 2007,
before natural movement "was even really defined." He showed it to an online contact, "Barefoot"
Ted McDonald, who in turn showed it to freelance journalist Christopher McDougall (later the author
of *Born to Run*). McDougall pursued an 11-page, 16-photo feature article on Le Corre's approach in
Men's Health — described as unusual attention for someone with, in Le Corre's words, "no form of
recognition" or credentials at the time. McDougall is also credited with suggesting the video's
title, though the magazine ultimately used a different title for the article itself.
sections.heading: How the video reached a mainstream audience

sections.body:
`[07:12]`–`[09:17]` Le Corre states the video's goal was not to impress but to give people
"permission to go outside and to jump and land and crawl and roll and balance and vault," naming
social conventions ("never the right place, never the right time... you're going to get dirty") as
the barriers keeping people from movements he calls "entirely our birthright." He also describes a
recurring reaction from early workshop attendees: movements that look effortless on video turn out
to be much harder in practice, which he frames as revealing that looking easy is itself evidence of
trained technique, not an absence of real skill.

**Erwan Le Corre frames MovNat as a systematic training method (not unstructured outdoor
activity) built on the premise that natural movement — not specialized sport — is the ancestral
foundation all human physical capability is derived from, and that movement requiring real
problem-solving produces different physiological/neurological effects than repetitive, "mindless"
exercise.** `[11:13]` "It is none of those disciplines, sports, protocols, programs [that] enable
natural movement. It's the other way around. Natural movement is what makes any sports, any
physical activity, any traditional physical discipline possible."

sections.body:
`[01:01]`–`[03:05]` Le Corre's stated founding rationale: natural movement training didn't exist in
a structured form ("it was missing... very very few people" trained that way), so he built a
method modeled on how martial arts are actually learned — through progressions with trained
teachers, not improvisation — applied to "running, jumping, landing, hanging, climbing, lifting and
carrying, throwing, catching."
sections.heading: Why MovNat exists: technique and conditioning applied to natural movement

sections.body:
`[08:11]`–`[10:12]` Le Corre traces a chain of reasoning from lactate research (Brooks's lactate
shuttle) — lactate as an actively used fuel crossing the blood-brain barrier, possibly a preferred
fuel for axons — toward a speculative conclusion he states outright is not yet established: "this
is not a substantiated theory... I imagine it'll come out and say, oh, lactate is the precursor to
your happiness." He separately cites brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) as a known
exercise-triggered effect, but stresses that "not any exercise is equal": only movement demanding
active engagement with "the here and now of the movement situation" is claimed to raise BDNF
production more than movement that is "just physical activity" — which he's careful to note is not
itself a bad thing.
sections.heading: Movement, lactate, and BDNF: a stated hypothesis, flagged as unsettled

concepts: segmental spinal movement — the idea that a stretch should be distributed evenly across every vertebral segment (base of skull to lower back) rather than concentrated in the most flexible area
movements: extension (prone lying): from forearms, pressing up onto the wrists while looking upward to extend the upper back, steering the extension away from the lower back or neck if felt there, then holding an extended position for 10 seconds using upper-back strength rather than pressing hard off the ground

flexion (rocking): forward-flexing the spine into a "C" shape (upper back, then mid/lower back, then hips) and rocking gently using minimal arm/leg momentum, then holding a full flexed position for 10 seconds

rotation: seated on an elevated bolster (hips above knee height) for a neutral spine, then reaching backward in sequence (head, then torso, then arm), holding an end-range rotation for 10 seconds using the body's own muscular tension rather than pulling with the opposite hand
principles: "the key to success of mobility is more about frequency or consistency than it is about intensity" — light, frequent daily practice recommended over occasional intense stretching

awareness and visualization (imagining the spine as a pole or ladder) are presented as more responsible for gained mobility than the stretch itself, since they direct effort toward stiff segments rather than over-stretching already-mobile ones

**Spinal mobility is trained here through three natural movements — rotation, flexion (rocking),
and extension (prone lying) — with the source's stated key principle being that consistent, light,
frequent practice combined with body awareness produces better results than infrequent, intense
stretching.** `[15:24]` "The key to success of mobility is more about frequency or consistency than
it is about intensity... lower the intensity, increase the frequency."

`[00:00]`–`[06:08]` Sitting on an elevated bolster so the hips are at or above knee height keeps the
spine neutral (rather than already flexed) before rotating. The reach sequence is deliberate — head
turns first, then torso, then the arm — visualized as a segmented pole or ladder twisting evenly
along its length, "from the base of your skull to your lower back," rather than concentrating
rotation in the neck or upper back alone. The final rep of each side is held for 10 seconds using
the person's own muscular tension rather than pulling on the opposite knee, on the stated logic
that self-generated end-range strength is preferable to relying on external leverage.

spine is like a C, the easier it is going to be to rock without needing to throw our arms and limbs
... around." The flexion sequence works upper back, then mid/lower back, then the hips, addressing
a stated common pattern where "the upper back will be rounded but the lower back will be tight,"
producing a jarring rather than smooth rock.

back or the neck is described as a sign the mid/upper back "isn't doing its job," and the
practitioner should back off and consciously redirect the extension there instead of pushing
further into the already-mobile segment.

**Gaspard Nouaille describes discovering the "natural method" of physical education — after a
childhood and youth built entirely around conventional sport (tennis, running, football, rugby,
etc.) — as "a revelation," and frames its value over conventional sport/fitness training as
reconnecting movement to a real purpose, taught through storytelling and group engagement rather
than isolated repetitions.** `[02:01]` "It's been quite a revelation for me because I didn't know
that natural movement at all at that time. I only did sports, and well, it's quite different,
actually."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:00]`–`[02:01]` Gaspard's background is "a background of conventional sport" (tennis, climbing,
running, athleticism, handball, football, rugby, volleyball). In 2020, running physical education
at a Montessori school in France, he found conventional sport "not enough" and sought out a family
teaching Georges Hébert's natural method — a different lineage from Hébert's own descendants,
per the transcript. `[04:03]` He later discovered MovNat in 2023 at a Biarritz training and
completed a Level 3 training in Vienna in 2024, describing MovNat as adding "a lot of really
interesting tools and skills" to adapt the roughly hundred-year-old natural method "to the actual
needs" of modern people.
sections.heading: From conventional sport to the natural method to MovNat

sections.body:
`[08:06]`–`[09:08]` Asked about cultural resistance to natural movement, Gaspard says it can seem
"a bit odd" because "it's not in our culture." The interviewer extends this with his own
experience training without machines: "people always looking at me like, 'What the hell is this
guy doing?'" He traces the resistance partly to a purpose-disconnection built into conventional
fitness: **"When you look at like traditional functional fitness, it's like I'm deadlifting... Why?
I'm deadlifting to get stronger. It's never I'm deadlifting to be able to take something from point
A to point B."**
sections.heading: Why natural movement feels "odd," and conventional fitness's missing "why"

sections.body:
`[10:08]` For people unused to being outdoors, Gaspard starts indoors, working on the ground
"because they are not used to get up and sit down anymore" — calling MovNat's ground get-up
exercises "a really good addition" to the natural method. `[12:10]`–`[13:11]` For groups, the
natural method deliberately uses storytelling ("we have to face a danger, we have to pass through
an obstacle, we have to climb into a tree") to create a shared mood that gets participants
attempting movements without consciously deciding to: "they were not thinking they could do it, but
they just do it... they are just like, 'Whoa, what just happened?'"
sections.heading: Storytelling, group training, and get-ups as an entry point

sections.body:

families: throwing and balancing. The interviewer extends the balance point with his own framing:
apparent simplicity ("stand on one leg... that's easy") gives way to real difficulty, and losing
balance is tied to losing focus on unrelated thoughts — "the next thing you know they're thinking
about the meeting they have to have at 3:00 and then they start to fall."

**Coaching a large, mixed-ability natural-movement group without losing anyone rests on five
stated practices: give simple homework, make progressions bite-sized and achievable, watch body
weight shift closely, personalize each person's progression within the shared group movement, and
make it fun and explicitly tied to real life.** `[24:26]` Summarized directly: "the most important
thing to have as a coach is the ability to progress and regress for your clients within that
program setting" and "the last piece is just make it fun, make it enjoyable, and meet your
participants where they are in the middle."

sections.body:
`[01:00]`–`[03:03]` Elaine Hung describes running MovNat classes for a year out of a CrossFit
facility with low uptake: **"when they recognized that they actually cannot squat as the grass or
like sit and squat... they very quickly just fade away and went back to what they are used to."**
The stated reason is a mindset mismatch — CrossFit culture is described as rewarding pushing "until
you collapse," which conflicts with a mobility-first approach that asks people to slow down. The
gym's resulting positioning: **"we really want to stay in between where we are training mobility...
and also give you strength that is practical for your everyday life... we are not trying to
replace the CrossFit, Hyrox, or the... yoga, Pilates kind of stuff."**
sections.heading: Why the gym stopped trying to convert CrossFitters

sections.body:
`[07:08]`–`[08:08]` Classes are built as a pyramid: **mobility as the base** ("understanding that
you do not have range, and how do you expand the range"), **strength built on that available
range**, then **efficiency** (dynamic, explosive movement — jumps, vaults), with a play-based class
at the top. The stated logic: "if your base of mobility is not strong, it's not wide enough,
whatever you build is just going to be like narrow and small" — a wide base is framed as necessary
to support a large pyramid (i.e., long-term capability) later.
sections.heading: The class-structure pyramid

sections.body:
`[15:16]`–`[21:22]` Asked for top recommendations for coaching groups, Hung lists five in order:
(1) **give simple homework** movements practiced between sessions, since twice-weekly attendance
alone produces slow progress; (2) **make movements accessible** in achievable, bite-sized steps,
since visibly "clunky" early attempts at a hard movement can discourage people from continuing; (3)
**have a sharp eye** for body weight shift and muscle recruitment, correcting even a small angular
error, described as what "sets us apart from every other studio"; (4) **personalize progressions
within the group**, so faster and slower participants both stay safely challenged rather than
either stagnating or risking injury by keeping pace; (5) **make it fun and relatable to life
outside the gym** — connecting a movement to a concrete daily task like picking up a child or
groceries.
sections.heading: Five coaching tips for group settings

competency." He notes explicitly that this doesn't cover everyone ("you have people who can't get
off the ground but can squat 600 lb. I've seen it"), so it's offered as general guidance rather than
a complete diagnostic.

sections.body:
**Loren Fjord argues parkour is not "the most extreme" human movement but rather ordinary
movements — walking, balancing, running, jumping — practiced to a high skill level on
unpredictable terrain, and that natural movement training of this kind benefits older adults more
than the young, because a lost or gained capability is far more consequential later in life.**
`[14:17]` "I would actually challenge that definition to say that parkour is actually the most
simple human movements, and then you are witnessing a practitioner that has taken the basic human
movements to the extreme." `[17:20]` "Who benefits most is going to be the elderly, the older
person, the adult. Because as you have more skill and more balance, it is more consequential in
your life what you can and can't do."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[15:17]`–`[16:19]` Fjord's own stated distinction: "gymnastics is attempting at or building to the
most complex human movements over the most measured and metered and sterile terrain... the exact
same vault whether you're in China or... the US." Parkour, by contrast, is "every scenario, every
handrail... every fire hydrant, retaining wall, wherever you are... at the subjective whims of
Mother Nature or an architect that did not have you in mind." Both disciplines are said to "start
very basic," with elite expression in either looking extreme only at the top.
sections.heading: Parkour vs. gymnastics: terrain as the defining difference

sections.body:
`[19:22]` A specific case is described: an elderly client recovering from a back injury wanted to
play with her grandson but was afraid, telling Fjord "I'm scared that I won't be able to get up off
the floor." After being taught a prone get-up and a tripod get-up, "her whole life shifted at that
moment... she was like, 'This was the most useful thing I've ever done.'" Fjord's own conclusion
from this: **"it's not about performance, it's about confidence."**
sections.heading: The elderly get-up anecdote: confidence over performance

sections.body:
`[19:22]`–`[20:23]` Both speakers describe assessing a client's "lowest level of competency" before
programming rather than assuming capability from appearance. A contrasting cautionary story is
given: a trainer put a client who "looked like they were in shape" but lacked coordination straight
onto 18-inch box jumps; the client missed the jump, "went shin first into a wooden box, broke the
shin, went over, broke the oval, dislocated the shoulder."
sections.heading: Assessing competency before programming — and what happens when you skip it

sections.body:
`[11:13]`–`[12:14]` A quality heuristic Fjord attributes to a coach named Michael Carr: "if you're
trying to figure out whether your client's doing it right... the easiest test is the poop test.
Does it look like shit?" — used as an accessible proxy for whether a movement is under control and
therefore safer. Separately, Fjord cites *Biotensegrity* by Graham Scarr to push back on treating
the body as fragile: **"there's like this working assumption that we work like an inanimate object
that has a finite number of uses rather than a living tissue that replaces virtually all the cells
in its body over the course of 7 years."**
sections.heading: The "poop test" and biotensegrity: two proxies for safe, efficient movement

sections.body:
`[22:24]`–`[24:27]` Fjord recounts buying a one-way ticket to England 20 years ago after seeing a
parkour video, with no contacts, phone, or return plan, and being immersed in a mixed-skill
community including figures he names as among the sport's originators (Daniel Ilabaca, Phil Doyle,
pre-Storror-crew members). He credits this experience with three lasting effects: physical practice
as a "proxy" for broader life growth, "physical empathy" from training alongside vastly different
skill levels, and a habit of testing internal beliefs against physical reality. The video's final
third (from roughly `[24:27]` onward) is largely a promotional announcement for a 20th-anniversary
retreat event Fjord is organizing — included here for context, not treated as a movement-science or
practice claim in its own right.
sections.heading: Founder's origin story (context, not a movement-science claim)

like taking an entire movement category and saying it's completely off limits for the rest of your
life."** The described treatment was regression, not argument: starting the hip hinge from a
half-kneeling position so the patient could "integrate it and see that it's perfectly safe," then
progressing to the loaded kettlebell deadlift once trust was established — with the patient
reporting she felt her hamstrings working, not her back, and no pain.

sections.body:
**David Weck argues human movement should be trained around the spine as the origin of force and
coordination — not braced into a "neutral" position and treated as one joint — building an
evolutionary narrative from fish undulation through amphibian, mammalian, and primate movement
strategies to argue that multi-axis spinal mobility, not isolated "mirror muscle" strength, is the
foundation of both power and injury resistance.** `[07:13]` "I start noticing all these people are
coming to work with me who are physical therapists and they're personal trainers and they cannot
move their spine outside of this neutral and then they get hurt all the time." `[07:13]` His stated
reasoning is explicitly evolutionary rather than literature-first: "it's more of this thing of
like, what's the evolutionary perspective — why in the world does the spine have all of these
capabilities if you're not supposed to use them?"
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[63:32]`–`[76:48]` Weck states the upper body, not the feet, is where balanced movement is
organized: **"balance begins in the upper body... if my upper body is not correct then it doesn't
matter what my feet do."** His stated mechanism is neurological speed and degrees of freedom:
"it's a lot faster" to send a signal from the cervical spine than the lumbar spine, and the head
"has so many more degrees of freedom to align you precisely than your feet, legs, ankles." He
extends this into a definition of balance itself as coordination: "I define the word balance —
it's coordination."
sections.heading: "Balance begins in the upper body"

sections.body:
`[79:54]`–`[86:01]` Weck (with Kelley) discusses a specific contrast: sprinters are said to minimize
time on the ground to maximize flight time and stride length, while a named NFL athlete, Tyreek
Hill, is described as spending roughly 80% of his sprint time on the ground — time Weck frames as
valuable precisely because "you have more degrees of freedom to change the behavior of the system"
while still in contact with the ground, versus committing to a ballistic, uncorrectable path in the
air. Straight-line sprinting itself is characterized as a "fifth gear" that was "nonessential for
survival... a contrived thing to race you," since outrunning a predator is described as neither the
evolved strategy nor, per Weck, ever actually attempted: `[87:02]` "the caveman did not run away
from the saber-tooth tiger... you get your buddies, you all talk, you line them up... you point
your sticks at him."
sections.heading: Ground-contact time: sprinting versus multidirectional movement

sections.body:
`[08:13]`–`[16:27]` Weck builds a chain of evolutionary speculation — from an ocean-bound
"spinal engine" originating in lateral fish undulation, through amphibians (a locked degrees-of-
freedom "coiling" mechanism), to mammals bringing limbs under the body, to primates entering trees
and developing an upright, throwing-capable shoulder and chest structure. He is explicit that this
chain of reasoning is not settled science: `[08:13]` "at this point it's just a theory... evolution,
it's a theory that is wrong that is useful for the mental gymnastics of understanding yourself."
Kelley separately corrects one specific point in Weck's account, noting current understanding
attributes hominid ground-dwelling more to climate-driven fragmentation of rainforest into savanna
than to social competition in the trees `[15:26]`.
sections.heading: An evolutionary account of upright movement, offered as a hedge, not a fact

caption track leaves unanchored past this last timestamp. Referencing Georges Hébert's ten
natural-method categories (walk, run, jump, climb, move on all fours, balance, swim, lift, throw,
defend), Weck describes reorganizing them into locomotion, manipulation, interaction, and combat,
and separately distills manipulative-movement training down to three original tools: **"the rod,
the rope, and the rock"** — using stone-lifting and carrying in place of a barbell deadlift on the
stated grounds that a stone "is going to have a little more carry over to what you do" than a gym
implement.
sections.heading: Movement taxonomy: from Hébert's ten categories to "stick, rope, rock"

`[44:06]`–`[52:16]` Weck describes struggling with irritable bowel syndrome since adolescence, and
during a period of marital separation, undertaking internal family systems therapy and an
MDMA-assisted therapy session in which he experienced hours of physical shaking he connects to
previously unprocessed trauma from sexual abuse in his early teens. He frames this experience
through his own movement vocabulary — deep postural ("tonic") muscles as a site where unresolved
emotion gets stored, loosely connecting it to Nikolai Bernstein's concept of tone as the most basic
layer of motor control. **This is presented throughout as Weck's own therapeutic and personal
experience, not a scientific or biomechanical claim** — he offers no study connecting muscular tone
to trauma storage, and the note preserves that distinction rather than treating it as established.

**The instructor's stated purpose in this session is not to teach the Turkish get-up as an
exercise, but to use it to demonstrate that tools and added load (a kettlebell, a 100 lb sandbag)
are teaching constraints that make a fundamental movement — standing up from lying down — more
learnable and efficient, not the source of the physical adaptation itself.** `[01:03]` "The tool

sections.body:
`[19:24]`–`[21:26]` The instructor frames all human movement as falling into domains: **manipulative**
("I manipulate my environment or myself around the environment... pick up something... point A to
point point B"), **locomotive** (getting from point A to point B without necessarily picking
anything up), **combative** (striking and grappling), and **expressive** ("I can move just because
I want to"). Get-up patterns are placed on the combative side of this map but are said to transfer
everywhere: "every get-up that you've ever seen in your life happens in grappling in some way or
another," citing the "shin box" stretch, "S-mount," and "octopus guard" as the same body positions
appearing in a different context.

`[02:04]`–`[03:06]` The get-up is used specifically because "it teaches all the foundational
principles of human movement, which are tension and relaxation," and "how your points of support...
interact with the surface of support," with points of support diminishing (and stability
decreasing) as the body moves from lying down toward standing. The instructor teaches the sequence
in discrete named steps — body weight shift (rocking to the side), body weight transfer (onto
elbow, then hand), and the half-kneeling stand — coaching each student individually and adjusting
cues (e.g., "drive out of this foot," using momentum from a kicking leg) based on where each
student struggles.

100 lb turning into 40."** The general principle stated: "as you load it, I'm always trying to make
sure that I'm loading my skeleton versus my tissue" — added intensity is reframed as a tool that
can reduce, not just increase, difficulty when applied correctly.

**A formal running-mechanics comparison scored minimalist-shoe running at 4.03 and fully barefoot
running at 2.26 (lower being better) for the same runner, illustrating that even a minimalist shoe
measurably alters mechanics compared to bare feet — but the source stresses that going barefoot
requires gradually built tolerance, not an immediate switch.** `[00:00]` "This was your score with
the minimalist shoes on... 4.03. The closer you get to 1.2, the better. This is you running
completely barefoot... 2.26."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[08:10]` The physical therapist's proposed mechanism: **"having a shoe... was increasing your
threat response to the ground"** — a shoe raises tolerance for harder impact by dulling tactile
feedback, so the body drives into the ground harder; barefoot, "it's got to be a little bit more
careful... a lot more sensitive to what's happening." This is offered as personal interpretation in
conversation, not a cited study finding.
sections.heading: Why footwear changes mechanics: the "threat response" explanation

sections.body:
`[03:04]`–`[05:08]` A first-hand account of switching to barefoot shoes describes a full-body
soreness reaction after a single 12-hour shift in them, followed by a gradual capacity-building
approach: balance work (elevated and low surfaces, split squats), and alternating short bouts of
barefoot running with rowing, biking, or ski-erg intervals rather than running continuously.
`[05:08]`–`[07:09]` Skipping this buildup is named as the cause of hairline fractures, plantar
fasciitis, stress fractures, and Achilles tendinitis in runners generally. `[06:09]`–`[07:09]`
Environment matters as much as pace: barefoot running on hot Miami asphalt with sharp debris is
called out directly as unsuitable, versus natural surfaces like grass.
sections.heading: Building tolerance safely, and where barefoot running doesn't make sense

sections.body:
`[11:12]`–`[13:13]` Practical drills from a "natural movement perspective": toe yoga, toe drops,
toe rainbow, short-foot arch lifts, walking on the inside/outside of the feet, heel walking,
balancing and picking up small objects (a hacky sack) with the foot, low-level plyometric pogo
hops, and deep kneeling positions that load toe extension.
sections.heading: Foot-strengthening drills demonstrated

sections.body:
Overuse injuries from progressing barefoot training too quickly: hairline fractures, plantar
fasciitis, stress fractures, and tendinitis (peroneal, tibialis posterior, Achilles).

sections.body:
**Miriam Lancewood recounts living eight years (from 2010) in the wild mountains of New Zealand's
South Island with her partner, hunting, gathering, and moving nomadically with no fixed camp, and
attributes to that lifestyle a set of self-reported changes: reawakened senses, reduced long-term
anxiety despite situational fear remaining, physical strength and fitness maintained without
formal exercise, and a repeatable roughly-two-week period of mental "slowing down" on first
entering that way of life.** `[05:07]`–`[06:08]` "We decided that... we would go and give all the
belongings away... and go with our backpack to live in the wilderness... I learned how to hunt with
a bow and arrow and we hunted... gathered and we collected the plants... we have done this since
2010."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[09:10]`–`[12:14]` A typical day is described as: waking before sunrise, exploring new terrain
(since the couple stayed nomadic rather than settling), hunting on foot by scanning the landscape
for the color or movement of a hare or deer rather than active chasing, returning to camp to cook
and eat organ meat fresh, an afternoon walk following whichever stream or ridge looked interesting,
and sleeping when it got dark. `[12:14]`–`[13:16]` Lancewood explicitly ties this to circadian
rhythm: "we go to bed when it's dark and really sleep when it's dark and wake up when it's light,"
noting she wakes repeatedly on full-moon nights because of the added natural light.
sections.heading: Daily life: nomadic, hunting-based, and unscheduled

sections.body:
`[08:10]`–`[09:10]` Lancewood reports specific sensory changes she attributes to years of
hunting-dependent living: "my sense of smell is increased enormously because I need it for
hunting... my vision, looking in the far distance... my hearing has improved so much," extending
the claim to her older partner Peter as well. She frames city life as actively suppressing these
senses rather than the senses being lost: **"the city is very desensitizing, but the opposite
happens in nature."**
sections.heading: Senses "coming back": a stated but self-reported reversal

sections.body:
`[14:17]`–`[16:19]` Lancewood describes an initial period of boredom and restlessness lasting "about
[two weeks]" before her mind's pace matched nature's, required "in order for the mind to calm down."
Notably, the podcast host (running an unrelated wilderness-immersion program) interjects that this
matches what they independently observed in their own students without having discussed it with
Lancewood beforehand: "I always say there's gonna be a two-week period where your mind is gonna
have to slow down... it seems to happen almost to each person without fail." This is two
independent (though both informal, non-controlled) sources converging on the same figure, which is
worth noting as stronger than either account alone, while still being anecdotal rather than
measured.
sections.heading: The two-week adjustment, corroborated independently

sections.body:
`[19:22]`–`[20:24]` Lancewood distinguishes wilderness fear as short-term and situational (real
physical risk — a storm, a fall) from what she describes as the free-floating, long-term anxiety
she associates with city life, reporting that public speaking to large audiences (a new part of her
life after publishing a book) no longer triggers fear for her. `[37:42]`–`[38:42]` She traces one
specific, easy-to-miss cause of that anxiety to background noise, recounting noticing anxiety while
sitting in a field and tracing it to a distant person using a "whipper snipper" (string trimmer):
"this machine noise has bad effects on us and we're not aware of it because it's happening all the
time... I think it has really bad side effects on all our mental health."
sections.heading: Fear, anxiety, and an unnoticed cause: noise

sections.body:
`[30:36]`–`[31:38]` Lancewood explicitly describes going into the wilderness expecting to
reconnect with animist/spiritual beliefs she grew up with (reincarnation, nature spirits), and
instead becoming "more and more pragmatic" and no longer believing in those specific frameworks —
while separately describing later experiences (she references one involving "connecting with a
plant") that she states plainly she has no vocabulary for: "it doesn't fit in their religion... I
haven't really got words for it." This is a clear, source-stated hedge that should travel with the
claim rather than be resolved into either "she found spirits" or "she found nothing."
sections.heading: Spirituality: starting pragmatic, ending without a name for it

sections.body:
Self-reported physical changes: increased strength, thicker hair ("one-third thicker"), and
maintained fitness without formal exercise, attributed to a wild-meat diet and daily walking with a
loaded pack. `[18:20]` Psychological: reduced long-term anxiety and fear, described as a side
effect rather than a deliberately trained outcome.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

None beyond descriptive phrases used informally in the conversation (e.g. "the art of doing
nothing"), which are conversational framing rather than defined technical terms.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- Fear as behaviorally contagious "like sheep" passing panic to lambs, used to argue that humans
  retain the same instinct — "we're so conditioned to think, oh, I'm afraid, what am I afraid of...
  where does that come from? Oh, those people over there, they are afraid." `[33:40]`–`[34:41]`
- A described shared perceptual experience: both Lancewood and her partner reported the world
  looking "very gray and dull" while near a passing stranger, then switching back to normal once he
  left — offered explicitly as a strange, hard-to-explain anecdote about consciousness rather than
  a claimed general phenomenon. `[31:38]`–`[32:39]`
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
**Entirely first-person lived experience and self-report, not technique instruction or a
controlled study.** Physical claims (strength, hair thickness, fitness) are Lancewood's own
unverified self-observation. Sensory and psychological claims (heightened senses, reduced anxiety)
are subjective self-report with no measurement. The "two-week adjustment" claim is unusually
corroborated by a second, independent informal source (the podcast host's own program), which
raises its credibility above a single anecdote but still falls short of a measured or
peer-reviewed claim. The spirituality discussion is explicitly hedged by the speaker herself as
something she cannot name or fit into an existing framework — that hedge is preserved above rather
than resolved.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
Converges with `NlQE1zMJwns` ("What Traditional Sports Couldn't Teach Me") and `EmN2ON_VIXY` ("The
Next Evolution of MovNat") on the broader premise that modern civilization suppresses inherent
human capacities that a return to more natural conditions can restore — but this note is a
first-person "I actually lived this way for years" account, distinct in kind from those two videos'
coaching/organizational framing, and involves no MovNat-style structured technique or method.
`CIShtax3_nI` ("Behind The Scenes with Erwan Le Corre") similarly frames modern life as suppressing
an innate "birthright" capacity, which this account's sensory-reawakening claims independently
echo from a completely different, non-MovNat source — worth noting as two unrelated sources
converging on a similar idea, though neither is a controlled or measured claim.
